summary30s: Independent India chose a 'Mixed Economy' model, combining capitalist private enterprise with socialist public sector commanding heights.
The Bombay Plan (1944) saw industrialists jointly demand state investment; the Planning Commission was established in March 1950 with PM as chairman.
The First Five Year Plan (1951-56), drafted by economist K.N. Raj, focused on agriculture, irrigation (Bhakra Nangal), and land reforms.
The Second Five Year Plan (1956-61), drafted by P.C. Mahalanobis, emphasized rapid industrialization, heavy capital goods, and import tariffs.
The Green Revolution transformed food security via HYV wheat/rice seeds and tube-wells, while the White Revolution (Operation Flood, Verghese Kurien) created the Amul dairy cooperative model.

coreConcepts.title: Ideas of Development and the Bombay Plan (1944)
coreConcepts.explanation: Two developmental models existed in 1947: the liberal-capitalist model (US/Western Europe) and the socialist model (USSR). Nehru and most nationalists favored socialist planning. Surprisingly, big Indian industrialists also favored state-led development: in 1944, a group of prominent industrialists met in Bombay and drafted the 'Bombay Plan', urging the government to make major investments in industrial and other economic infrastructure. In March 1950, the Government of India established the Planning Commission by a cabinet resolution (extra-constitutional body), with the Prime Minister as its ex-officio Chairman.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: Politics in India Since Independence, Chapter 3, Section 1 & 2
coreConcepts.examTip: The Bombay Plan was drafted in 1944 by industrialists demanding government intervention. Planning Commission set up in March 1950.

coreConcepts.title: First FYP (K.N. Raj) vs Second FYP (P.C. Mahalanobis)
coreConcepts.explanation: The First Five Year Plan (1951-1956) sought to lift the country out of poverty. Young economist K.N. Raj argued that India should 'hasten slowly' for the first two decades. The plan prioritized the agrarian sector: huge investments were made in large dams (Bhakra Nangal, Hirakud) and irrigation, alongside tenancy land reforms. The Second Five Year Plan (1956-1961), drafted under the leadership of statistician Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis, stressed rapid industrialization and heavy industries. The 1956 Industrial Policy Resolution declared that the state would control the 'commanding heights' of the economy. High tariffs were imposed on imports to protect domestic industries.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: Politics in India Since Independence, Chapter 3, Section 3 & 4
coreConcepts.examTip: First FYP = K.N. Raj (Agriculture/Dams); Second FYP = P.C. Mahalanobis (Heavy Industry/Public Sector).

coreConcepts.title: Key Controversies: Agriculture vs Industry & Gandhian Alternatives
coreConcepts.explanation: Debate erupted between agriculture and industry advocates. Leaders like Charan Singh (who later formed Bharatiya Lok Dal) argued that industrialization diverted resources away from rural farming, impoverishing the peasantry. Others argued that industrialization was indispensable to relieve agrarian overcrowding. J.C. Kumarappa, a Gandhian economist, proposed an alternative blueprint called 'Economy of Permanence', emphasizing village industries, small-scale production, and environmental sustainability. Meanwhile, the 'Kerala Model' proved that high social indicators (literacy, life expectancy, low infant mortality) could be achieved through public healthcare and education even with low per capita income.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: Politics in India Since Independence, Chapter 3, Section 5
coreConcepts.examTip: J.C. Kumarappa authored 'Economy of Permanence' based on Gandhian economic principles.

coreConcepts.title: The Green Revolution and Operation Flood (White Revolution)
coreConcepts.explanation: Facing chronic food shortages and humiliation under the US PL-480 wheat import scheme in the mid-1960s, the government launched the 'Green Revolution'. Supported by scientist M.S. Swaminathan and Agriculture Minister C. Subramaniam, the state provided High Yielding Variety (HYV) seeds, subsidized fertilizers, pesticides, and assured water to farmers in fertile regions. Wheat production soared, making India self-sufficient in foodgrains. However, it had social costs: benefits were geographically concentrated in Punjab, Haryana, and Western UP, widening disparities between rich farmers and landless laborers. Concurrently, Verghese Kurien ('Milkman of India') pioneered the cooperative dairy movement at Anand (Gujarat), creating Amul and launching 'Operation Flood' (White Revolution) in 1970, making India the largest milk producer.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: Politics in India Since Independence, Chapter 3, Section 6
coreConcepts.examTip: Verghese Kurien is known as the 'Milkman of India'; Operation Flood launched rural dairy cooperatives.

Who was the economist who drafted the Second Five Year Plan, giving it a heavy-industry and public-sector orientation?
(A) K.N. Raj
(B) P.C. Mahalanobis
(C) J.C. Kumarappa
(D) Amartya Sen
workedExamples.explanation: The Second Five Year Plan (1956-61) was drafted by a team of economists and planners under the leadership of P.C. Mahalanobis, founder of the Indian Statistical Institute.

commonTraps.misconception: Thinking the Planning Commission was created by an Act of Parliament or mentioned in the Constitution.
commonTraps.correctConcept: The Planning Commission was NOT a constitutional body, NOR was it created by an act of parliament. It was set up in March 1950 by a simple executive cabinet resolution.
commonTraps.whyTrapWorks: Questions ask 'Is the Planning Commission a constitutional, statutory, or extra-constitutional body?'
commonTraps.cuetWarning: Planning Commission was an extra-constitutional, non-statutory body.

commonTraps.misconception: Assuming the Green Revolution benefited all Indian farmers equally.
commonTraps.correctConcept: The Green Revolution was deliberately targeted at well-endowed agricultural regions (Punjab, Haryana, Western UP) with irrigation, widening regional and class inequalities.
commonTraps.whyTrapWorks: Options claim it solved poverty uniformly across eastern and southern India.
commonTraps.cuetWarning: Green Revolution created severe regional disparities and peasant polarization.

practiceQuestions.question: In which year was the Planning Commission of India established by a resolution of the Union Cabinet?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Planning Commission was set up in March 1950 by a simple resolution of the Government of India.

practiceQuestions.question: Who was the young economist associated with drafting the First Five Year Plan who argued that India should 'hasten slowly'?
practiceQuestions.explanation: K.N. Raj, a young economist involved in drafting the plan, argued that India should 'hasten slowly' for the first two decades.

practiceQuestions.question: The Second Five Year Plan placed primary developmental emphasis on:

options.text: Heavy industries and capital goods production

practiceQuestions.explanation: The Second Plan stressed on heavy industries. It was drafted by a team of economists led by P.C. Mahalanobis.

practiceQuestions.question: Who among the following founded the cooperative dairy movement in Anand (Amul) and was known as the 'Milkman of India'?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Dr. Verghese Kurien played a crucial role in the story of Gujarat Cooperative Milk Marketing Federation Ltd. (Amul) and was nicknamed the 'Milkman of India'.

practiceQuestions.question: The 'Kerala Model' of development is globally renowned for achieving which of the following outcomes?

options.text: Highest growth rate of heavy manufacturing industries
High human development indicators (education, health, low IMR) despite low per capita income
Completely unregulated free market private capitalism
Highest agricultural yields of wheat in South Asia

practiceQuestions.explanation: The 'Kerala model' focused on education, health, land reform, effective food distribution, and poverty alleviation despite low industrial growth.

practiceQuestions.question: Which Gandhian economist authored the work 'Economy of Permanence' proposing rural-centric industrial planning?
practiceQuestions.explanation: J.C. Kumarappa, a chartered accountant and economist, authored 'Economy of Permanence' based on Gandhian principles.

practiceQuestions.question: In 1944, what was the joint proposal drafted by prominent Indian industrialists demanding state-led investment in industrial infrastructure called?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A section of big industrialists met in 1944 and drafted a joint proposal known as the 'Bombay Plan'.

practiceQuestions.question: Which of the following states was the primary geographic beneficiary of the initial phase of the Green Revolution in the late 1960s?

options.text: Punjab, Haryana, and Western Uttar Pradesh

practiceQuestions.explanation: Regions like Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh became agriculturally prosperous, while others remained backward.

practiceQuestions.question: Which US agricultural import scheme was India humiliatingly dependent upon during the severe food crises of 1965-1967?
practiceQuestions.explanation: India was dependent on food aid, mainly from the United States under the PL-480 program.

practiceQuestions.question:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R):
Assertion (A): The Second Five Year Plan imposed substantial import tariffs and protective barriers on foreign goods.
Reason (R): The Mahalanobis strategy aimed to protect nascent domestic heavy industries from global competition and promote import substitution.

options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)

practiceQuestions.explanation: High tariffs on imports protected domestic producers from foreign competition, encouraging indigenous heavy manufacturing. Both are true and (R) explains (A).
